newsitem.title: POLAND: SOLIDARITY CHIEF DEMANDS GODLY POLISH CONSTITUTION.
newsitem.headline: SOLIDARITY CHIEF DEMANDS GODLY POLISH CONSTITUTION.

text.p: Solidarity union chief Marian Krzaklewski flung the left-dominated parliament's ideas for a new Polish constitution in its face on Tuesday and demanded that Poles be offered a charter enshrining religious values.

Krzaklewski called, in an address to parliament, for the rightist union's own proposal for a constitution to be put to voters in a referendum, alongside a secular draft agreed by four main parliamentary parties of the centre and left.

"Poland has always founded its system of values and its constitutional law on Christian values," Krzaklewski told both houses of parliament, gathered as the national assembly for a second reading of the new constitution bill.

Poland has had a temporary interim constitution since soon after the Solidarity movement, backed by the Roman Catholic Church, toppled Communist rule in 1989 and rendered the previous Stalinist-era national charter obsolete.

The draft now proposed by parliament reflects the fact that the current legislature, elected in 1993, is dominated by the secular-minded ruling ex-communists while the right has less representation than its wide popular support might now warrant.

A Solidarity-led alliance leads in opinion polls and hopes to come top in elections late this year and the union charges that the parliamentary parties are trying to force through their own constitutional version before then.

The right submitted its own draft constitution two years ago, and wants this to be offered for people to choose, alongside the parliamentary draft, in a constitutional referendum before or alongside the elections.
Parliament says it may consider some Solidarity amendments to its draft and therefore invited Krzaklewski to put its views, but insists only one version should go to referendum.

The key differences between the parliamantary and rightist "Citizen's" draft of the constitution revolve largely around how Poles view themselves -- similar issues to those which will dominate campaigning in the coming elections.
They hark back to pre-1989 divisions when the Church was a focus for democratic protest against the atheist ruling party.

Solidarity, arguing that Poles have for centuries been overwhelmingly a Catholic nation, want the constitution to start with a ringing invocation of God and to recognise that Christian principles take precedence over man-made laws.

The compromise parliamentary draft, approved by some centrist Christians who opposed pre-1989 communist rule such as former Prime Minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki, stresses that the nation is made up both of believers and non-believers.
Among other issues, Solidarity wants the constitution to guarantee the right to life right from conception, going against the current parliament's decision last year to ease restrictions on abortion.
Krzaklewski, who plans to run for parliament in this year's polls, later told reporters his speech had been a call to tough talks rather than outright confrontation.
But his fighting talk evoked irritation in parliament.
"Saying he did not want confrontation, Krzaklewski is doing everything to ensure that confrontation takes place," PAP news agency quoted opposition chief Mazowiecki as telling reporters.
